The general appearance of the built habitat will not have changed greatly, but there is likely to be much more solar and wind power hardware visible in the habitat and many communities and corporate campuses will boast their recently achieved energy independence. Electric and autonomous vehicles will start coming into their own, beginning to take the lead in new vehicle sales. Drivers in some cities and communities will begin noticing such impacts as greater ease of finding parking spaces and traffic relief. Tiny House communities and live/work loft developments will have become mainstream and proliferated on the suburban periphery, possibly driving the trailer park model into obsolescence--where it isn't obsolete already. In cities adaptive reuse will be seen as conventional as the urban real estate market begins to realize the hazard of building specialization. The 'lofting' movement that was once focussed on abandoned warehouses, industrial buildings, and urban waterfronts of the early 20th century will move to the repurpose of commercial buildings of the end and turn of that century as office/information automation advances white collar job destruction. Suburban corporate campuses may be abandoned and repurposed as low income communities or novel eco-villages. Urban farming will have greatly expanded, but before tall vertical farms appear, they will also repurpose commercial space, existing rooftops, and waterfronts with the growth of farming barges. Europe--long before the US--will approach parity in urban farming with China. (which today meets most urban produce demand within their cities)

In the area of computing and communications, the desktop PC will become largely obsolete, persisting only as special workstations and custom gaming systems. (dominated by VR gaming) It's nearly there today, but even all-in-one monitors and laptops will be pushed aside with the advance of hand-held computing power, improved WiFi, and emergent virtual cloud computing platforms. Most users will rely on collections of mobile devices and network appliances, the concept of the personal computer as a specific piece of hardware supplanted by the notion of a dispersed personal computing and communications cloud accessed by many, sometimes specialized, front-end devices.

A new class of 'virtual' corporations will emerge; companies that have no physical facilities of any kind and own nothing physical. Instead, they will contract all activity supporting them and hire workers who are Digital Nomads working at home or at co-working centers. We may see the first self-owned virtual companies that exist as smart-contracts and programs on the Blockchain and which, using simple sets of rules, manage their activity and maintenance--interface to the physical world--entirely through digital contracting. This is among the trends that will drive the obsolescence of so much commercial real estate in the larger built habitat, as location and white-collar manpower become increasingly irellevant.

Retail will continue its steady decline and increasingly fade in presence from the habitat as online sales matched to increasingly sophisticated distribution and delivery (with the emerging benefit of automated vehicles) obsolesces the store-front. The Big Box store that once supplanted small local retail and killed the giant shopping malls will itself be supplanted by highly automated Big Box warehouses built to buffer distribution for companies like Amazon. Eventually though, the business model of Amazon may be supplanted by the use of automated distribution networks as a kind of Internet of Stuff run as a public utility. This because the development and support of such large infrastructures is not well suited to the scope of just one company--even as large as Amazon. It is more suited to 'marketplace' business models like that of China's Taobao. So try to imagine Amazon being obsolesced by Amazon Market with a burgeoning localized seller community and hosting many other fulfilment, distribution, and storage services like personal storage, personal product subscriptions, personal mail and parcel shipping, local food delivery, just-in-time components distribution, even waste management and recycling. An open global network for stuff.

Another likely change in commerce is the emergence of accommodations automation by adoption of the Albergo Diffuso model with the growth of models like Airbnb. This will radically change the way accommodations work and may cause the obsolescence of many traditional hotels. We tend to think of 'automation' in the context of robots replacing human jobs. And so when we think of an automated hotel or resort we imagine places like the Strange Hotel in Japan where all the usual human roles are replaced by an assortment of funky robots. But that's not usually how automation impacts our culture. What is actually now emerging in hotel automation and will likely be common in a decade is something very disruptive, changing the whole concept of a hotel itself. Albergo Diffuso means 'dispersed hotel' and it's a concept first adopted in Italy to aid the transformation of dying medieval towns into tourist resorts. Houses and rooms across the towns were converted into hotel suites and to use them you would go to a main office in the town to check-in. This may sound similar to Airbnb, the difference being that the front desk is a web site, but the Airbnb model is not quite as automated as it could be. There's still a lot of dealing with people. What is needed, and which is likely to appear in mere months from now, is a viable Internet-linked smartlock that can be operated by smartphone. With that we can completely automate the payment and check-in/out process through mobile communications. Then to top it off we 'uberize' the housekeeping service so it too can function in a dispersed and on-demand manner. So once you've done this, you've eliminated the monolithic construct of the traditional hotel. Every spare space can be put online as a hotel room, temporarily or permanently and radically reduced the minimum investment to get into the accommodations business. And many other kinds of services can integrate to that same network. This is starting to happen now, and may become ubiquitous in a decade.

So there's a few of the interesting changes I anticipate in the near future.
